screens.title: Advanced Boot Process Control and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will take control of the Linux boot sequence from GRUB2 through systemd, and learn practical recovery techniques you can use in production and lab environments. You will learn how GRUB2 loads the kernel and the initramfs, how to safely edit kernel parameters at boot for troubleshooting, when and how to regenerate initramfs images with dracut, and how to use emergency and rescue modes to recover from failures. We will also practice diagnosing common boot failures such as filesystem corruption and missing kernel modules, and then implement GRUB password protection to reduce risk from unauthorized boot edits. A concrete example you will follow later is appending systemd. unit=emergency. target at the bootloader to land in a minimal shell and run fsck on the root partition. A common misconception is that a reboot always fixes boot issues; in reality, many failures require targeted edits to the kernel command line or rebuilding the initramfs. By the end of these screens you will know the exact files and commands to inspect, how to regenerate images, and how to choose between emergency and rescue modes during recovery. Consider which step you would try first if a server shows "VFS: Unable to mount root fs" — that question will guide our troubleshooting flow.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Advanced Boot Process
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Advanced Boot Process Control and Troubleshooting

Take control of GRUB2, the initial RAM filesystem, and systemd rescue targets so you can diagnose and recover systems that fail to boot.

GRUB2: load kernel & initramfs
initramfs & dracut: early drivers
Recovery modes: emergency/rescue
Explore Key Topics
Runtime GRUB Edits
Temporary kernel parameters like rd.break and systemd.unit=emergency.target let you inspect early boot without persistent change.
Rebuild initramfs
Use dracut to generate initramfs with drivers needed to mount your root filesystem after hardware or storage changes.
Secure GRUB
Add superuser and PBKDF2 hashed password entries to prevent unauthorized boot edits.
Visual Concept
Boot flow snapshot
BIOS/UEFI → GRUB2 → initramfs → kernel mounts root → systemd targets
This board uses terminal-first examples and command callouts so you can practice safely in virtual machines.
Start Here
Follow the upcoming lessons in order: understand GRUB files, practice runtime edits, learn initramfs regeneration, exercise emergency and rescue modes, then secure GRUB.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives define the practical skills you'll gain. First, you will configure GRUB2 to modify kernel parameters and boot options for troubleshooting. That means editing temporary runtime parameters at the GRUB menu and making persistent changes in /etc/default/grub followed by regenerating grub. cfg, so you can control a system's boot behavior safely. Second, you will understand the role of the initramfs and dracut in the early boot process: what files and modules must be present to mount the real root filesystem, how dracut detects required drivers, and when to regenerate the initramfs image after hardware or configuration changes. Third, you will perform system recovery using emergency and rescue modes, learning the difference in capabilities and when to remount root read-write or chroot into your system for deeper repairs. Finally, you will diagnose and resolve common boot failures including filesystem corruption and missing kernel modules, and implement GRUB password protection to prevent unauthorized edits. Each objective pairs a command-level task with a reasoning skill so you can both act and explain your choices during recovery.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practical application: diagnosing the root cause of boot failure, choosing the right recovery target, and performing secure configuration changes. You will practice identifying symptoms — for example, a kernel panic that indicates missing modules versus read-only filesystem errors that suggest corruption. You will learn the concrete sequence of actions to recover a failed boot: use GRUB runtime edits to drop into rd. break or emergency shell, inspect /proc and /dev to confirm device availability, remount root read-write if necessary, run fsck on unmounted devices, and regenerate initramfs with dracut when drivers are missing. You will also validate GRUB configuration problems by chrooting from a live environment and reinstalling GRUB. Lastly, we emphasize secure practices: generate a PBKDF2 hash with grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2, add set superusers and password_pbkdf2 entries to your custom grub script, and then rebuild grub. cfg. Each skill ties a command to a decision: why you chose emergency vs rescue, or when to regenerate the initramfs. That decision-making is what distinguishes an operator from an engineer.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Learning Objectives
Decision & Diagnosis
  • Map symptoms to likely causes: "VFS: Unable to mount root fs" often means missing modules in initramfs.
  • Use runtime GRUB edits to inspect the early environment without committing changes.
  • Prefer rescue.target for chroot workflows; emergency.target for minimal shell when you only need minimal fixes.
Safe change practices
  • Regenerate grub.cfg after editing /etc/default/grub with grub2-mkconfig.
  • Rebuild initramfs after hardware or driver changes using dracut.
  • Test GRUB password in a VM to avoid locking out administrators.

screens.title: GRUB2: role and configuration files
screens.narratorSegment: GRUB2 is the bootloader responsible for loading the kernel and the initial R A M filesystem before the kernel tries to mount the real root. Its behavior is driven by generated configuration files: grub. cfg in /boot/grub2 or under /boot/efi/EFI/ on UEFI systems. That grub. cfg file is commonly generated from templates and snippets in /etc/default/grub and /etc/grub. d. Editing /etc/default/grub allows you to set default kernel command-line options, timeouts, and other defaults. For example, a typical kernel parameter string might include rhgb quiet on some distributions. A useful recovery trick is to use the GRUB menu at boot and press e to edit the kernel line temporarily — that modification affects only the current boot. A common misconception is to edit grub. cfg directly; on most systems grub. cfg is regenerated and your edits will be overwritten. Instead, make persistent adjustments by changing /etc/default/grub or adding scripts under /etc/grub. d and then running grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub. cfg to apply them. A concrete example: if you add rd. break to the kernel command line at boot, you’ll drop into an early initramfs shell that allows inspection before the root filesystem is mounted. A takeaway: treat grub. cfg as generated output and manage intent through the source configuration and the runtime edit capability.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › GRUB2: role and configuration files
Definition
GRUB2 loads the kernel and initramfs into memory and hands control to the kernel. Configuration is generated, not usually hand-edited, so use /etc/default/grub and /etc/grub.d for persistent changes.
Key files
  • /boot/grub2/grub.cfg (or /boot/efi/EFI/<distro>/grub.cfg)
  • /etc/default/grub — default kernel command-line and options
  • /etc/grub.d/ — scripts that generate boot menu entries
Common mistake
Editing grub.cfg directly is overwritten by grub2-mkconfig; change sources then regenerate.
Runtime example
• Press 'e' at GRUB menu
• Find the line starting with linux or linuxefi
• Append rd.break or systemd.unit=emergency.target
• Press Ctrl+x or F10 to boot
Supporting notes
  • Temporary edits affect only the current boot and are safe for testing fixes.
  • Persistent changes require editing /etc/default/grub and running grub2-mkconfig -o <path>.
Key Takeaway

Treat grub.cfg as generated output; use source files and runtime edits for safe troubleshooting.

screens.title: Editing kernel parameters at boot
screens.narratorSegment: Knowing how to make temporary kernel parameter edits at the GRUB menu is essential for diagnosing early boot issues. The process is simple: when the GRUB menu appears, press e to edit the default entry, locate the linux or linuxefi line that contains the kernel path and existing parameters, append the token you need — for troubleshooting examples include rd. break to enter an initramfs shell, single for single-user mode, or systemd. unit=rescue. target to boot into rescue — and then press Ctrl+x or F10 to boot with those changes. This edit affects only the current boot, which makes it safe for experimentation. A concrete example: if the system reports "VFS: Unable to mount root fs", appending rd. break drops you into the initramfs before the root is mounted so you can inspect /dev and kernel modules. A frequent misconception is that these edits persist; they do not. After you find a working parameter you should make persistent changes in /etc/default/grub and regenerate grub. cfg. Finally, remember keyboard differences on VMs and consoles: the exact key to boot may vary, but the concept of runtime editing is universal. Will this method always fix the problem? No — but it often gives the diagnostic visibility you need.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Editing kernel parameters at boot
Step-by-step
  1. Interrupt GRUB menu and press e to edit the boot entry.
  2. Find the line beginning with linux or linuxefi.
  3. Append the desired parameter, for example rd.break or systemd.unit=emergency.target.
  4. Boot the modified entry with Ctrl+x or F10.
Temporary edits are fast and reversible, ideal for diagnosing device visibility, module loading, or early mounts.
Concrete example
# At GRUB editor, append:
systemd.unit=emergency.target
# Or for initramfs inspection:
rd.break
Misconception: Temporary edits persist. They do not; use /etc/default/grub for persistent changes.
Pro tip

Try runtime edits in a VM first to confirm behaviour before making persistent changes on production systems.

screens.title: initramfs and dracut
screens.narratorSegment: The initramfs is a small temporary root filesystem loaded into memory by GRUB2 before the kernel mounts the real root. Its job is to provide the kernel with the tools and drivers needed to find and mount the persistent root filesystem: storage controller drivers, LVM and RAID support, and any cryptographic modules required for encrypted volumes. If the initramfs omits a necessary driver, the kernel will be unable to find the root device and you might see errors like "VFS: Unable to mount root fs". On many distributions dracut is the tool that assembles the initramfs image. Dracut inspects the running system and includes modules and files it determines are necessary for boot. When you add new hardware, change disk controllers, or update kernel modules, you may need to regenerate the initramfs so the image contains the matching drivers. The chapter recommends using sudo dracut -f /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r). img $(uname -r) to rebuild the image for the current kernel. A common mistake is forgetting to rebuild initramfs after kernel or driver changes, which leads to boot failures. The takeaway: ensure your initramfs contains all modules your root filesystem depends on, and regenerate it after relevant changes.

keyIdea.title: initramfs essence
keyIdea.text: initramfs carries early userspace and drivers needed to locate and mount the real root; dracut generates this image based on current system requirements.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › initramfs and dracut
What initramfs contains
  • Essential kernel modules for storage controllers and filesystems.
  • Tools to assemble and mount the real root (LVM, RAID helpers, cryptsetup).
  • A minimal userspace for early troubleshooting when dropped into initramfs shell.
If these components are missing, the kernel cannot access the device that holds the root filesystem, resulting in mount failures and panics.
Regenerate with dracut
sudo dracut -f /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r).img $(uname -r)
Concrete scenario: After installing a new storage controller driver, regenerate initramfs so the driver is included at boot time.
Misconception: Rebooting will add missing drivers automatically. It will not; you must rebuild the initramfs to include them.
Key Takeaway

Always rebuild initramfs after kernel, driver, or storage changes to ensure the early boot environment can mount root.

screens.title: Emergency Mode vs Rescue Mode
screens.narratorSegment: Emergency mode and rescue mode are two distinct recovery targets provided by systemd, and choosing between them depends on the depth of repair you need. Emergency mode provides the most minimal environment: a single shell with the root filesystem usually mounted read-only, and very few services started. It is typically used when systemd cannot mount critical components and you need low-level access immediately; you can enter it by appending systemd. unit=emergency. target to the kernel command line. Rescue mode is more functional: it mounts a minimal set of local filesystems and starts a small subset of services; you will usually be asked for the root password before getting a shell. Rescue mode is preferable when you need to run multiple tools, reset passwords, or mount filesystems and chroot into the system for repairs. A concrete example: use emergency. target if the kernel cannot find devices and you need to remount root read-write and run fsck; use rescue. target when you plan to reset a forgotten root password or reinstall GRUB from a semi-functional environment. A common misconception is that rescue mode is always safer; in fact, emergency mode is sometimes required to stop services from interfering with repairs. Decide based on whether you need minimal isolation or more utilities and mounted filesystems.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Emergency Mode vs Rescue Mode
Emergency Mode
Minimal shell, root often read-only, very few services. Enter with systemd.unit=emergency.target. Use it to remount root, perform fsck, and inspect devices when mounts fail.
  • Use when systemd cannot mount root or essential components.
  • Remount root read-write with: mount -o remount,rw /
Rescue Mode
A more functional rescue environment that mounts local filesystems and starts a small set of services. Enter with systemd.unit=rescue.target. Often prompts for root password and is suitable for chroot workflows and password resets.
  • Ideal for chrooting and reinstalling GRUB from a live environment.
  • Offers more utilities but may start services that interfere with low-level repairs.
When to pick emergency
Device discovery or mount failures needing immediate isolation.
When to pick rescue
When you need a broader environment to run tools and chroot.
Misconception check
Rescue isn't always safer; choose based on toolset vs isolation needs.

screens.title: Diagnosing filesystem corruption and repair
screens.narratorSegment: Filesystem corruption is a common boot failure symptom. It often manifests as read-only mounts, input and output errors, or kernel panics. The safe sequence is to avoid running fsck on a mounted filesystem; instead, boot into emergency or a rescue environment where the affected filesystem is unmounted, then run fsck. A practical approach from a VM or rescue shell: identify the root partition with df -h / or lsblk, remount root read-write if you are in emergency to inspect, then reboot into a rescue environment or use a live image so the filesystem is not active, and run fsck -y /dev/sda1 (replace with the actual device). The -y flag automates repairs but use it with caution; in production you may prefer interactive repair to review actions. A frequent misconception is that rebooting will correct corruption; it may make matters worse if repairs are attempted on mounted volumes. After successful fsck and repair, reboot and observe the boot sequence. If the problem recurs, investigate underlying causes such as failing disks or incorrect shutdown sequences. The takeaway: perform fsck only on unmounted filesystems and prefer rescue/live environments for safe repair.

keyIdea.text: Do not run fsck on mounted filesystems; use emergency/rescue or a live environment to unmount and repair with fsck safely.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Diagnosing filesystem corruption and repair
Workflow
  1. Confirm partition: df -h / or lsblk to find the device.
  2. Boot into emergency or use a live USB so the filesystem is unmounted.
  3. Run fsck -y /dev/sda1 (replace device) to perform repairs.
  4. Reboot and confirm normal boot behavior.
Example command
fsck -y /dev/sda1
Concrete note: On LVM or encrypted volumes, unlock and deactivate layers before fsck on the underlying block device.
Misconception: Running fsck on a live root can corrupt data. Always unmount first.
Key Takeaway

Use unmounted environments for fsck; prefer interactive checks in critical systems to review proposed repairs.

screens.title: Recovering from missing kernel modules
screens.narratorSegment: When the kernel cannot mount the root filesystem because required drivers are missing from initramfs, the visible symptom is often a panic or inability to locate block devices. The correct recovery is to rebuild the initramfs so it includes the necessary modules. If you can boot a compatible kernel or live image, chroot into the installed system and run dracut to regenerate the image for the appropriate kernel version. The chapter provides the canonical command: sudo dracut -f /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r). img $(uname -r). If you cannot boot at all, use a rescue image, mount the root filesystem, chroot, and run dracut there. After rebuilding, ensure grub. cfg points to the correct initramfs and kernel, then reboot. A common misconception is that reinstalling the kernel always fixes missing-modules boot errors; reinstalling may help, but failing to rebuild initramfs for the target kernel will still leave the early boot environment incomplete. The concrete example: after adding a new storage driver module, regenerate initramfs so that driver is available before the kernel attempts to mount root. The takeaway: dracut must be run in the context of the target system so it can detect and include the right modules.

keyIdea.title: Missing modules fix
keyIdea.text: Rebuild the initramfs with dracut for the target kernel, doing so from a chroot or live environment if the system won't boot normally.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Recovering from missing kernel modules
When modules are missing
Kernel cannot access devices needed for root. Symptoms include "VFS: Unable to mount root fs" or early panics.
  • Boot a live or rescue image if the installed system won’t start.
  • Mount and chroot into the installed root before regenerating initramfs.
  • Run dracut to include the necessary drivers for your kernel.
Rebuild command
sudo dracut -f /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r).img $(uname -r)
Concrete example: After installing a new storage controller, chroot into the system and run the dracut command for the running kernel so the driver is present at boot.
Misconception: Reinstalling the kernel alone will ensure modules are present. Unless initramfs is rebuilt, the early boot environment may still lack drivers.
Key Takeaway

Always regenerate initramfs after adding modules or changing hardware so required drivers are present in the early boot image.

screens.title: Recovering from incorrect GRUB configuration
screens.narratorSegment: An incorrect grub. cfg or damaged GRUB installation can prevent the kernel from loading. When that happens, boot from a live CD or rescue USB and mount your installed root filesystem and the EFI or /boot partition as needed. Then chroot into the installed system so you operate in the same environment as the target system. From the chroot you can regenerate grub. cfg using grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub. cfg (or the UEFI path), reinstall the bootloader if necessary, and verify that kernel and initramfs paths are correct. A typical sequence is: mount /dev/mapper/centos-root /mnt, mount /boot and /boot/efi to /mnt/boot and /mnt/boot/efi, then chroot /mnt and run grub2-mkconfig and grub2-install if required. A common misconception is that copying a working grub. cfg from another system will always work; differences in device naming, UUIDs, or partition layout can make that dangerous. The concrete repair is to rebuild configuration within the context of the target system so scripts in /etc/grub. d and /etc/default/grub generate a consistent grub. cfg. After reinstalling GRUB and regenerating grub. cfg, unmount and reboot to validate the repair.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Recovering from incorrect GRUB configuration
Chroot-based recovery steps
  1. Boot a live USB and mount the installed root and boot partitions under /mnt.
  2. Mount virtual filesystems: /dev, /proc, /sys into the chroot environment.
  3. Chroot into /mnt and run grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg and grub2-install if needed.
  4. Exit, unmount, and reboot to verify success.
Commands (chroot context)
mount /dev/sda2 /mnt
mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/boot
for fs in /dev /proc /sys; do mount --bind $fs /mnt$fs; done
chroot /mnt
sudo grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
# optionally: grub2-install /dev/sda
exit
Concrete caution: Use the target system's /etc/grub.d and /etc/default/grub so generated grub.cfg matches your layout.
Misconception: Copying grub.cfg from another host can break boot due to differing UUIDs and paths.

screens.title: GRUB password protection
screens.narratorSegment: GRUB password protection prevents an attacker with physical access from editing boot entries to gain root. Implementing it involves generating a PBKDF2 hashed password using grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2, then adding set superusers and password_pbkdf2 entries to a custom script under /etc/grub. d, such as /etc/grub. d/40_custom. After making that change you must regenerate grub. cfg with grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub. cfg so the protected entries appear in the generated configuration. A concrete workflow: run sudo grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2, enter a strong password, copy the produced grub. pbkdf2. sha512... hash, append lines like set superusers="cohortia" and password_pbkdf2 cohortia to the 40_custom file, make that file executable, then regenerate grub. cfg. A critical security note from the chapter: GRUB protection helps against modifications via the GRUB menu but does not replace physical security; an attacker with a live USB or by resetting firmware could bypass GRUB protections. A common mistake is failing to test the password in a VM first — you might accidentally lock yourself out. The takeaway: use PBKDF2 hashed passwords and test changes in a controlled environment before applying in production. GRUB password protection means generate a pbkdf2 hash, add superuser and password_pbkdf2 lines in a custom grub script, mark it executable, and regenerate grub.cfg to apply protection.. In practical terms, how to add pbkdf2 hashed passwords and restrict boot edits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › GRUB password protection
Steps to secure GRUB
  1. Generate a PBKDF2 hash: sudo grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2 and copy the output.
  2. Edit /etc/grub.d/40_custom to add set superusers and password_pbkdf2 entries.
  3. Make the custom file executable and regenerate grub.cfg with grub2-mkconfig -o <path>.
Example snippet
sudo tee -a /etc/grub.d/40_custom > /dev/null <<EOF
set superusers="cohortia"
password_pbkdf2 cohortia grub.pbkdf2.sha512.10000.A1B2C3...
EOF
sudo chmod +x /etc/grub.d/40_custom
sudo grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
Concrete caution: Test the password in a VM before applying to production to avoid accidental lockout.
Misconception: GRUB password equals full physical security. It does not—live media and firmware resets can bypass it.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: simulate fsck and secure GRUB
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity is intended for a VM or test environment. First simulate a filesystem check on next boot by creating /forcefsck on the root partition with sudo touch /forcefsck and then reboot. Observe whether fsck runs and, if the system drops to emergency, use the GRUB runtime edit to append systemd. unit=emergency. target or press 'e' and add rd. break to inspect the initramfs. In emergency mode remount root read-write with mount -o remount,rw / and run fsck -y on the affected device, replacing /dev/sda1 with your partition. After repairs, reboot normally. Second, implement GRUB password protection: run sudo grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2, copy the hash, append set superusers and password_pbkdf2 entries to /etc/grub. d/40_custom, chmod +x it, and regenerate grub. cfg with grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub. cfg. Reboot to see the GRUB prompt require credentials for edits. A common mistake is doing this on a production host without testing; always validate in a VM first. content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Lab walkthrough
Step A — Force fsck
sudo touch /forcefsck
sudo reboot
# If dropped to shell, remount and run fsck:
mount -o remount,rw /
fsck -y /dev/sda1
Observe the boot messages. If the system hangs, use GRUB runtime edits to enter emergency or rd.break for early inspection.
Step B — Secure GRUB
sudo grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2
# copy the hash
sudo tee -a /etc/grub.d/40_custom > /dev/null <<EOF
set superusers="cohortia"
password_pbkdf2 cohortia <PASTE_HASH>
EOF
sudo chmod +x /etc/grub.d/40_custom
sudo grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
sudo reboot
Test that attempting to edit a boot entry now requires the username and password you configured.
Safety reminder
Always perform these steps in a VM first. Mistakes to GRUB configuration can make a host unbootable.

screens.title: Commands you'll use repeatedly
screens.narratorSegment: This slide collects and explains the core commands you'll run during boot troubleshooting so you have a mental model of what each does. grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub. cfg regenerates the boot configuration using /etc/default/grub and scripts in /etc/grub. d; use it after editing defaults or adding custom entries. dracut -f /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r). img $(uname -r) forces dracut to recreate the initramfs image for the current kernel, ensuring required drivers are present. fsck -y /dev/sda1 runs an automated filesystem consistency check and attempts repairs; -y accepts fixes without prompt, which can be helpful in automation but should be used carefully. grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2 produces a PBKDF2 hash string suitable for password_pbkdf2 entries; copy the long hash into a custom grub script and then regenerate grub. cfg. A misconception to correct: these commands interact across layers — changing /etc/default/grub without running grub2-mkconfig leaves your system using old runtime options. A concrete example: after adding a driver and rebuilding initramfs, run grub2-mkconfig so the kernel line in grub. cfg points to the new initramfs. The takeaway: memorize the intent of each command and their correct context—live boot, chroot, or installed system—so you don't run them in the wrong environment.

Boot config

Generates grub.cfg from /etc/default/grub and /etc/grub.d. Always run after changing source files.

screens.narratorSegment: Keep these three action items close when you approach a boot failure. First, verify symptoms and choose the recovery target: emergency for minimal isolation or rescue for a richer environment. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will take control of the Linux boot sequence from GRUB2 through systemd, and learn practical recovery techniques you can use in production and lab environments. You will learn how GRUB2 loads the kernel and the initramfs, how to safely edit kernel parameters at boot for troubleshooting, when and how to regenerate initramfs images with dracut, and how to use emergency and rescue modes to recover from failures. We will also practice diagnosing common boot failures such as filesystem corruption and missing kernel modules, and then implement GRUB password protection to reduce risk from unauthorized boot edits. A concrete example you will follow later is appending systemd. unit=emergency. target at the bootloader to land in a minimal shell and run fsck on the root partition. A common misconception is that a reboot always fixes boot issues; in reality, many failures require targeted edits to the kernel command line or rebuilding the initramfs. By the end of these screens you will know the exact files and commands to inspect, how to regenerate images, and how to choose between emergency and rescue modes during recovery. Consider which step you would try first if a server shows "VFS: Unable to mount root fs" — that question will guide our troubleshooting flow.

These objectives define the practical skills you'll gain. First, you will configure GRUB2 to modify kernel parameters and boot options for troubleshooting. That means editing temporary runtime parameters at the GRUB menu and making persistent changes in /etc/default/grub followed by regenerating grub. cfg, so you can control a system's boot behavior safely. Second, you will understand the role of the initramfs and dracut in the early boot process: what files and modules must be present to mount the real root filesystem, how dracut detects required drivers, and when to regenerate the initramfs image after hardware or configuration changes. Third, you will perform system recovery using emergency and rescue modes, learning the difference in capabilities and when to remount root read-write or chroot into your system for deeper repairs. Finally, you will diagnose and resolve common boot failures including filesystem corruption and missing kernel modules, and implement GRUB password protection to prevent unauthorized edits. Each objective pairs a command-level task with a reasoning skill so you can both act and explain your choices during recovery.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical application: diagnosing the root cause of boot failure, choosing the right recovery target, and performing secure configuration changes. You will practice identifying symptoms — for example, a kernel panic that indicates missing modules versus read-only filesystem errors that suggest corruption. You will learn the concrete sequence of actions to recover a failed boot: use GRUB runtime edits to drop into rd. break or emergency shell, inspect /proc and /dev to confirm device availability, remount root read-write if necessary, run fsck on unmounted devices, and regenerate initramfs with dracut when drivers are missing. You will also validate GRUB configuration problems by chrooting from a live environment and reinstalling GRUB. Lastly, we emphasize secure practices: generate a PBKDF2 hash with grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2, add set superusers and password_pbkdf2 entries to your custom grub script, and then rebuild grub. cfg. Each skill ties a command to a decision: why you chose emergency vs rescue, or when to regenerate the initramfs. That decision-making is what distinguishes an operator from an engineer.

GRUB2 is the bootloader responsible for loading the kernel and the initial R A M filesystem before the kernel tries to mount the real root. Its behavior is driven by generated configuration files: grub. cfg in /boot/grub2 or under /boot/efi/EFI/ on UEFI systems. That grub. cfg file is commonly generated from templates and snippets in /etc/default/grub and /etc/grub. d. Editing /etc/default/grub allows you to set default kernel command-line options, timeouts, and other defaults. For example, a typical kernel parameter string might include rhgb quiet on some distributions. A useful recovery trick is to use the GRUB menu at boot and press e to edit the kernel line temporarily — that modification affects only the current boot. A common misconception is to edit grub. cfg directly; on most systems grub. cfg is regenerated and your edits will be overwritten. Instead, make persistent adjustments by changing /etc/default/grub or adding scripts under /etc/grub. d and then running grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub. cfg to apply them. A concrete example: if you add rd. break to the kernel command line at boot, you’ll drop into an early initramfs shell that allows inspection before the root filesystem is mounted. A takeaway: treat grub. cfg as generated output and manage intent through the source configuration and the runtime edit capability.

Knowing how to make temporary kernel parameter edits at the GRUB menu is essential for diagnosing early boot issues. The process is simple: when the GRUB menu appears, press e to edit the default entry, locate the linux or linuxefi line that contains the kernel path and existing parameters, append the token you need — for troubleshooting examples include rd. break to enter an initramfs shell, single for single-user mode, or systemd. unit=rescue. target to boot into rescue — and then press Ctrl+x or F10 to boot with those changes. This edit affects only the current boot, which makes it safe for experimentation. A concrete example: if the system reports "VFS: Unable to mount root fs", appending rd. break drops you into the initramfs before the root is mounted so you can inspect /dev and kernel modules. A frequent misconception is that these edits persist; they do not. After you find a working parameter you should make persistent changes in /etc/default/grub and regenerate grub. cfg. Finally, remember keyboard differences on VMs and consoles: the exact key to boot may vary, but the concept of runtime editing is universal. Will this method always fix the problem? No — but it often gives the diagnostic visibility you need.

The initramfs is a small temporary root filesystem loaded into memory by GRUB2 before the kernel mounts the real root. Its job is to provide the kernel with the tools and drivers needed to find and mount the persistent root filesystem: storage controller drivers, LVM and RAID support, and any cryptographic modules required for encrypted volumes. If the initramfs omits a necessary driver, the kernel will be unable to find the root device and you might see errors like "VFS: Unable to mount root fs". On many distributions dracut is the tool that assembles the initramfs image. Dracut inspects the running system and includes modules and files it determines are necessary for boot. When you add new hardware, change disk controllers, or update kernel modules, you may need to regenerate the initramfs so the image contains the matching drivers. The chapter recommends using sudo dracut -f /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r). img $(uname -r) to rebuild the image for the current kernel. A common mistake is forgetting to rebuild initramfs after kernel or driver changes, which leads to boot failures. The takeaway: ensure your initramfs contains all modules your root filesystem depends on, and regenerate it after relevant changes.

Emergency mode and rescue mode are two distinct recovery targets provided by systemd, and choosing between them depends on the depth of repair you need. Emergency mode provides the most minimal environment: a single shell with the root filesystem usually mounted read-only, and very few services started. It is typically used when systemd cannot mount critical components and you need low-level access immediately; you can enter it by appending systemd. unit=emergency. target to the kernel command line. Rescue mode is more functional: it mounts a minimal set of local filesystems and starts a small subset of services; you will usually be asked for the root password before getting a shell. Rescue mode is preferable when you need to run multiple tools, reset passwords, or mount filesystems and chroot into the system for repairs. A concrete example: use emergency. target if the kernel cannot find devices and you need to remount root read-write and run fsck; use rescue. target when you plan to reset a forgotten root password or reinstall GRUB from a semi-functional environment. A common misconception is that rescue mode is always safer; in fact, emergency mode is sometimes required to stop services from interfering with repairs. Decide based on whether you need minimal isolation or more utilities and mounted filesystems.

Filesystem corruption is a common boot failure symptom. It often manifests as read-only mounts, input and output errors, or kernel panics. The safe sequence is to avoid running fsck on a mounted filesystem; instead, boot into emergency or a rescue environment where the affected filesystem is unmounted, then run fsck. A practical approach from a VM or rescue shell: identify the root partition with df -h / or lsblk, remount root read-write if you are in emergency to inspect, then reboot into a rescue environment or use a live image so the filesystem is not active, and run fsck -y /dev/sda1 (replace with the actual device). The -y flag automates repairs but use it with caution; in production you may prefer interactive repair to review actions. A frequent misconception is that rebooting will correct corruption; it may make matters worse if repairs are attempted on mounted volumes. After successful fsck and repair, reboot and observe the boot sequence. If the problem recurs, investigate underlying causes such as failing disks or incorrect shutdown sequences. The takeaway: perform fsck only on unmounted filesystems and prefer rescue/live environments for safe repair.

When the kernel cannot mount the root filesystem because required drivers are missing from initramfs, the visible symptom is often a panic or inability to locate block devices. The correct recovery is to rebuild the initramfs so it includes the necessary modules. If you can boot a compatible kernel or live image, chroot into the installed system and run dracut to regenerate the image for the appropriate kernel version. The chapter provides the canonical command: sudo dracut -f /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r). img $(uname -r). If you cannot boot at all, use a rescue image, mount the root filesystem, chroot, and run dracut there. After rebuilding, ensure grub. cfg points to the correct initramfs and kernel, then reboot. An incorrect grub. cfg or damaged GRUB installation can prevent the kernel from loading. When that happens, boot from a live CD or rescue USB and mount your installed root filesystem and the EFI or /boot partition as needed. Then chroot into the installed system so you operate in the same environment as the target system. From the chroot you can regenerate grub. cfg using grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub. cfg (or the UEFI path), reinstall the bootloader if necessary, and verify that kernel and initramfs paths are correct. A typical sequence is: mount /dev/mapper/centos-root /mnt, mount /boot and /boot/efi to /mnt/boot and /mnt/boot/efi, then chroot /mnt and run grub2-mkconfig and grub2-install if required. A common misconception is that copying a working grub. cfg from another system will always work; differences in device naming, UUIDs, or partition layout can make that dangerous. The concrete repair is to rebuild configuration within the context of the target system so scripts in /etc/grub. d and /etc/default/grub generate a consistent grub. cfg. After reinstalling GRUB and regenerating grub. cfg, unmount and reboot to validate the repair.

GRUB password protection prevents an attacker with physical access from editing boot entries to gain root. Implementing it involves generating a PBKDF2 hashed password using grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2, then adding set superusers and password_pbkdf2 entries to a custom script under /etc/grub. d, such as /etc/grub. d/40_custom. After making that change you must regenerate grub. cfg with grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub. cfg so the protected entries appear in the generated configuration. A concrete workflow: run sudo grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2, enter a strong password, copy the produced grub. pbkdf2. sha512... hash, append lines like set superusers="cohortia" and password_pbkdf2 cohortia to the 40_custom file, make that file executable, then regenerate grub. cfg. A critical security note from the chapter: GRUB protection helps against modifications via the GRUB menu but does not replace physical security; an attacker with a live USB or by resetting firmware could bypass GRUB protections. A common mistake is failing to test the password in a VM first — you might accidentally lock yourself out. The takeaway: use PBKDF2 hashed passwords and test changes in a controlled environment before applying in production. This slide collects and explains the core commands you'll run during boot troubleshooting so you have a mental model of what each does. grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub. cfg regenerates the boot configuration using /etc/default/grub and scripts in /etc/grub. d; use it after editing defaults or adding custom entries. dracut -f /boot/initramfs-$(uname -r). img $(uname -r) forces dracut to recreate the initramfs image for the current kernel, ensuring required drivers are present. fsck -y /dev/sda1 runs an automated filesystem consistency check and attempts repairs; -y accepts fixes without prompt, which can be helpful in automation but should be used carefully. grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2 produces a PBKDF2 hash string suitable for password_pbkdf2 entries; copy the long hash into a custom grub script and then regenerate grub. cfg. A misconception to correct: these commands interact across layers — changing /etc/default/grub without running grub2-mkconfig leaves your system using old runtime options. A concrete example: after adding a driver and rebuilding initramfs, run grub2-mkconfig so the kernel line in grub. cfg points to the new initramfs. The takeaway: memorize the intent of each command and their correct context—live boot, chroot, or installed system—so you don't run them in the wrong environment.

These compact reminders summarize what to carry forward. GRUB2 is the bootloader that places the kernel and the initramfs into memory; manage persistent settings via /etc/default/grub and regenerate grub. cfg rather than editing grub. cfg directly. Kernel parameters control boot behavior — use runtime edits to append rd. break, single, or systemd. unit=rescue. target for diagnostics without persistent change. The initramfs is the early userspace image that must contain drivers to access your root filesystem; rebuild it with dracut after relevant kernel, driver, or hardware changes. Keep these concise ideas in mind as a checklist when troubleshooting any boot issue: confirm symptoms, choose the right recovery target, repair or rebuild the early environment, and then secure access. Keep these three action items close when you approach a boot failure. First, verify symptoms and choose the recovery target: emergency for minimal isolation or rescue for a richer environment. Second, repair the early environment: run fsck on unmounted filesystems, chroot from live media to rebuild initramfs with dracut, and regenerate grub. cfg from your source files. Third, secure boot access: generate a PBKDF2 hash with grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2, add a superuser and password_pbkdf2 entry to a custom grub script, and rebuild grub. cfg; but remember this complements physical security, it does not replace it. Practically, use a VM to validate each change before applying it to production so you avoid accidental lockouts or persistent misconfigurations.
